title: Algorithms
overview: This chapter is the practical core of Paper 4. You must be able to write and trace linear search, binary search, bubble sort and insertion sort; implement stack, queue, linked-list and binary-search-tree operations; explain where graphs and dictionaries are suitable; and compare solutions using both time and space complexity. The examples below use executable Python and preserve the conditions and boundary checks that commonly earn marks.
syllabusPoints: Write and trace linear and binary searches, including the sorted-data requirement and changing search boundaries.
Write and trace bubble and insertion sorts, and explain how data size and initial order affect performance.
Find and insert items in linked lists and binary trees; insert and delete items in stacks, queues and linked lists.
Describe stacks, queues, linked lists, dictionaries, binary trees and graphs, including suitable implementations and uses.
Compare algorithms by time and memory use, expressing growth with Big O notation.

definitions.definition: A logical description of stored data and permitted operations, independent of the structure used to implement it.
A way to describe how an algorithm's time or memory requirement grows as input size n increases, ignoring constants and less significant terms.
A binary tree ordered so that keys smaller than a node occur in its left subtree and larger keys occur in its right subtree, according to a defined duplicate policy.
A last-in, first-out ADT whose main operations are push, pop and peek.
A first-in, first-out ADT whose main operations are enqueue at the rear and dequeue from the front.
Attempting to remove or read an item from an empty data structure.
Attempting to insert into a fixed-size data structure that has no free position.

sections.title: Linear search: reliable on any order
content: Linear search inspects each item until the target is found or every item has been checked. It works with unsorted data and is often the correct choice for a short list or a single search where sorting first would cost more than it saves.

The loop invariant is that every position before the current index has already been checked and does not contain the target. Returning -1 is a deliberate sentinel meaning not found; never use a normal index such as 0 for this because 0 can be a valid result.
bullets: Best case O(1): the first item matches.
Worst and average growth O(n): the target is late or absent.
Extra space O(1): only the index and target are needed.

examples.label: Linear search with a not-found result

sections.title: Binary search: halve a sorted search interval
content: Binary search requires data sorted using the same comparison rule as the search. It keeps inclusive lower and upper boundaries, compares the middle item, then discards the half that cannot contain the target. If low becomes greater than high, the interval is empty.
Using mid = (low + high) // 2 produces an integer index. The updates must be mid + 1 and mid - 1; assigning low = mid or high = mid can leave the interval unchanged and cause an infinite loop.
bullets: Each comparison removes about half the remaining candidates, giving O(log n) worst-case time.
Doubling the list size adds roughly one extra comparison, not twice as many.
Sorting has a cost, so binary search is strongest when the data is already sorted or will be searched repeatedly.

examples.content: low=0, high=5, mid=2 → 13 is too small, so low=3. Then low=3, high=5, mid=4 → 27 is too large, so high=3. Finally mid=3 → 18 is found.

sections.title: Bubble sort: adjacent swaps and early stopping
content: Bubble sort compares adjacent pairs and swaps a pair when it is in the wrong order. After one complete ascending pass, the largest unsorted value has moved to the end, so the inner loop can be shortened on the next pass.

A swapped flag records whether the pass changed anything. If no swap occurs, the whole list is already sorted and the algorithm can finish early. This improves nearly sorted input but does not change the O(n²) worst case.
bullets: Use a temporary variable or Python tuple assignment to perform the swap correctly.
Reset swapped to False at the start of every outer pass.
The final i positions are already fixed, so do not compare them again.

examples.label: Optimised bubble sort

sections.title: Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix
content: Insertion sort treats the first item as a sorted prefix. It stores the next item as key, shifts every larger prefix value one position right, and places key into the gap. Storing key before shifting prevents it from being overwritten.

Nearly sorted data needs few shifts and may approach O(n), while reverse-sorted data requires about n²/2 comparisons and shifts. It is in-place and stable when equal items are not moved past each other.
bullets: Start at index 1 because the one-item prefix at index 0 is already sorted.
The while condition needs both j >= 0 and values[j] > key.
Insert key at j + 1 after shifting finishes.

examples.label: Insertion sort with shifting

sections.title: Stacks and queues: protect the boundaries
content: The ADT specifies behaviour; the underlying list is only one implementation. A stack pushes and pops at the same end. A queue enqueues at the rear and dequeues at the front. Fixed arrays also require top/front/rear pointers and explicit overflow tests.

Removing index 0 from a Python list shifts later items and costs O(n). It is acceptable for demonstrating FIFO behaviour, but a circular array queue is more efficient because front and rear wrap around and no records are shifted.

An ADT can also be built from another ADT. A queue made from two stacks keeps new items in an input stack and moves them to an output stack only when needed. The reversal restores first-in, first-out order. One dequeue may cost O(n), but each item is moved at most once, so the average (amortised) cost per operation is O(1).
bullets: Check empty before pop, peek or dequeue to prevent underflow.
For a fixed-size implementation, check full before push or enqueue to prevent overflow.
Return the removed item when the caller may need it.

sections.title: Linked lists: change links without losing nodes
content: Each node stores data and a link to the next node. Search is sequential because a node can only be reached by following links from head. Inserting at the front is O(1); finding a location remains O(n).

For deletion, keep both current and previous. Deleting the head is a special case because head itself must change. For any other node, bypass it with previous.next = current.next. Changing links in the wrong order can make the rest of the list unreachable.
bullets: Use None as the null pointer/end marker in Python.
Insertion/deletion avoids shifting array elements, but each node uses extra memory for its link.
Searching an ordinary linked list remains O(n), even if insertion at the head is O(1).

examples.label: Find, insert and delete in a linked list

sections.title: Binary search trees: shape controls performance
content: Searching and insertion compare the target key with the current node and choose one subtree. A balanced tree has height proportional to log n, but a badly skewed tree has height n and therefore O(n) search. Never claim every BST is automatically O(log n).

The code below sends equal keys to the right. Another duplicate policy is possible, but search and insertion must apply the same rule. Returning the root from insertion is important because the first insertion creates a new root and recursive calls must reconnect changed child links.
bullets: In-order traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order.
A binary tree has at most two children per node; only a BST also enforces an ordering rule.
The syllabus requires search and insertion code for binary trees, not deletion code.

examples.label: Search and insert in a binary search tree

sections.title: Dictionaries and graphs: choose the right relationship
content: A dictionary stores unique keys mapped to values. Python dict gives average O(1) lookup, insertion and deletion, although this is not a worst-case guarantee. It is suitable when a meaningful key, such as candidate number, should retrieve a record directly.

A graph contains vertices and edges; edges may be directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted. Graphs model many-to-many connections such as roads, network links or dependencies. The syllabus requires describing and justifying graph use, but not writing a graph implementation.
bullets: An adjacency matrix gives O(1) edge checks but uses O(V²) memory.
An adjacency list is usually more memory-efficient for sparse graphs.
A dictionary models key-to-value lookup; a graph models connections between many vertices.

sections.title: Big O: compare growth, not stopwatch seconds
content: Time complexity counts how the number of significant operations grows with input size. Space complexity describes additional memory growth. O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n²) are growth classes, not exact running times.

A high-quality comparison states the relevant case and assumptions. For example, binary search is O(log n) only after the data is sorted, while linear search may be preferable for a tiny, unsorted list searched once. An in-place algorithm may save memory even if another algorithm is faster.
bullets: Drop constant factors and lower-order terms: 3n² + 8n + 4 is O(n²).
State whether you are discussing best, average or worst case when it changes the conclusion.
Compare algorithms solving the same task under the same input assumptions.

comparisonTable.title: Complexity and conditions worth stating
rows: Swap flag can stop an already sorted pass early
Useful for small or nearly sorted data

examTips: Write the precondition before binary-search code: the data must be sorted using the same comparison order.
Show boundary and empty/full checks in ADT code; these are visible correctness marks, not optional polish.
When tracing a sort, show the complete list after each pass rather than only listing swaps.
For a complexity comparison, name input size n, the case being discussed and any preprocessing or memory trade-off.
Test empty data, one item, target at each boundary, target absent and duplicate values.
commonMistakes: Updating binary-search bounds to mid instead of mid ± 1, so the interval may never shrink.
Overwriting insertion sort's key before shifting the larger values.
Popping or dequeuing without an underflow check.
Deleting the linked-list head without updating head.
Claiming every BST operation is O(log n), even when the tree is skewed.
Writing graph code when the question only asks for a justified representation or use.

quickRecall.question: What condition must hold before binary search?
quickRecall.answer: The data must be sorted using the same ordering rule used by the comparisons.

quickRecall.question: Why does binary search have O(log n) time?
quickRecall.answer: Each comparison discards about half of the remaining search interval.

quickRecall.question: What does the swapped flag do in bubble sort?
quickRecall.answer: It allows the algorithm to stop when a complete pass makes no swaps, proving the list is sorted.

quickRecall.question: Why is key stored before insertion-sort shifting begins?
quickRecall.answer: The value at that position will be overwritten while larger prefix items move right.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between stack and queue removal order?
quickRecall.answer: A stack is LIFO; a queue is FIFO.

quickRecall.question: When can BST search become O(n)?
quickRecall.answer: When the tree is badly skewed so its height grows to n.
